doc.title: Cedar Walton — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Dallas childhood, training and early playing
title: Beethoven's Moonlight sonata and Hanon as the key training book
summary: He struggled with the second movement of Beethoven's Moonlight sonata and says no other training book mattered as much as Hanon's endless exercises.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Among your teachers, before we get to university level, were there any uh, instructors that pointed you [inaudible – tape noise]?

Yeah, uh … Oh, I didn't mean to touch the mike. Beethoven's Midnight Sonata is a prime example of that in uh, first movement is a, a, memorable to me because it wasn't that difficult. Doo-doo-dee, Doo-doo-dee, Doo-doo-dee, DA-da-DA. You must have heard that, right? That part is easy but when it gets to the second movement [laughs] I struggled so hard with it, I just gave up, to tell you the truth. But that's what I'm supposed to be doin', telling the truth, but I'd hate to put us to [inaudible]. [laughs]
You mentioned [inaudible – overlapping sounds] question along these lines: As you go along, you talked about, from the beginning, exercise books …
Were there other books, um, training books that you, were important to you?

Not as important as Hanon, no. Hanon was the one that just … it had no pieces, it just had exercises, and they were endless, you know, like, it seemed to me at that time, you know, and probably would now, too, if I were going back to that. But that's a good question but … pieces themselves uh, uh, so, uh, so helpful with your approach to the keyboard, to the piano. It's just the way they're constructed. If you learn to play them, you, you're makin' a big stride in your development.
